questions.stem: Who led Australia's delegation at the Paris Peace Conference in 1919?
options: Stanley Bruce
Joseph Lyons
Andrew Fisher
Billy Hughes
questions.explanation: Prime Minister W. M. (Billy) Hughes represented Australia at Paris. Stanley Bruce became prime minister in 1923, and Andrew Fisher had resigned as prime minister in 1915.

questions.stem: Which outcome did Billy Hughes secure for Australia at the Paris Peace Conference?
options: A permanent seat on the Council of the League of Nations
A share of German colonies in Africa and the Pacific
A League of Nations C-class mandate over German New Guinea
Full annexation of German Samoa and of the Marshall Islands
questions.explanation: Hughes wanted outright annexation of German New Guinea but accepted a C-class mandate, which allowed Australia to govern it almost as part of its own territory. Samoa went to New Zealand as a mandate, and Australia never held a permanent Council seat.

questions.stem: Why did Hughes oppose Japan's proposal to include a racial equality clause in the League of Nations Covenant?
options: He believed Japan would use it to claim New Guinea
He wanted Britain to keep its alliance with Japan secret
He thought it would force Australia to admit German migrants
He feared it would threaten the White Australia policy
questions.explanation: Hughes saw the clause as a threat to Australia's right to control immigration under the White Australia policy, and he campaigned hard against it. The clause was not adopted, which caused lasting resentment in Japan.

questions.stem: Historians often see Australia's role at the Paris Peace Conference as a step towards independent nationhood mainly because:
options: Australia refused to sign the Treaty of Versailles and made a separate peace
Australia's delegates were seated alongside the great powers on the Council of Ten
Australia signed the Treaty of Versailles and joined the League in its own right
Australia was given control of British foreign policy in the Pacific region
questions.explanation: Hughes insisted that the dominions be represented separately, and Australia signed the treaty and became a founding member of the League of Nations in its own right, though as part of the British Empire delegation. It did not control British policy or sit with the great powers.

questions.stem: About how many Australians died as a result of service in the First World War?
options: about 6,000
about 250,000
more than 400,000
more than 60,000
questions.explanation: More than 60,000 Australians died, from a population of under five million, and many more were wounded. About 417,000 enlisted, so 'more than 400,000' describes enlistments rather than deaths.

questions.stem: What was the main aim of soldier settlement schemes after the First World War?
options: To settle returned soldiers in the mandated territory of Nauru
To give returned soldiers land to farm and develop rural areas
To give returned soldiers houses in the suburbs of capital cities
To train returned soldiers as factory workers in new industries
questions.explanation: State and Commonwealth schemes gave returned soldiers blocks of farm land, combining reward for service with the goal of populating and developing rural Australia. Many settlers failed because blocks were too small, land was poor, settlers lacked experience and prices fell.

questions.stem: Which combination of factors best explains why many soldier settlers had walked off their blocks by the 1930s?
options: Forced resettlement of the blocks for the Snowy Mountains Scheme
Small or poor blocks, inexperience, debt and falling prices
High prices, labour shortages and strict wartime price controls
A ban on selling produce overseas and the loss of all subsidies
questions.explanation: Many blocks were too small or on marginal land, settlers often lacked farming experience and capital, and debts grew as commodity prices fell in the 1920s and collapsed in the Depression. The Snowy Mountains Scheme did not begin until 1949.

questions.stem: In the 1919 Clothing Trades case, the Commonwealth Arbitration Court set the basic wage for women at about:
options: 54 per cent of the male rate
75 per cent of the male rate
90 per cent of the male rate
the same rate as for men
questions.explanation: Justice Higgins set the female basic wage at about 54 per cent of the male rate, on the reasoning that women did not support a family. Wartime regulations later raised many women's rates, and 75 per cent was adopted for federal awards in 1949-50.

questions.stem: Which development best shows the limits of change for women in Australia after the First World War?
options: Most women in wartime roles were expected to return to domestic life
Women gained the right to vote in federal elections for the first time in 1918
Women were admitted to the AIF as combat soldiers on the Western Front in 1918
Edith Cowan became the first woman elected to an Australian parliament in 1921
questions.explanation: Australian women had gained the federal vote in 1902, so 1918 is wrong, and they were not combat soldiers. Cowan's election in Western Australia in 1921 shows change. The expectation that women return to the home, along with lower wages, shows the limits.

questions.stem: The slogan 'Men, Money and Markets' summed up the development policy of which 1920s government?
options: the Scullin Labor government
the Lyons government
the Hughes government
the Bruce-Page government
questions.explanation: Stanley Bruce's Nationalist-Country Party coalition (1923-1929) aimed to develop Australia with British migrants, British loans and access to British markets. The Scullin Labor government took office in October 1929.

questions.stem: Which innovation of the 1920s most helped to overcome the isolation of people in outback Australia?
options: The building of the transcontinental railway to Darwin
The extension of electric trams to most country towns
Aviation, including the Flying Doctor service begun in 1928
The opening of the Sydney Harbour Bridge to road and rail traffic
questions.explanation: Air services such as Qantas, founded in Queensland in 1920, and the Flying Doctor service, which made its first flight from Cloncurry in 1928, reduced outback isolation. Radio broadcasting from 1923 helped too. The railway to Darwin was not completed until 2004.

questions.stem: How did the growth of manufacturing in the 1920s change where Australians lived?
options: It moved most of the population out into small country towns and farms
It caused the populations of Sydney and Melbourne to fall sharply
It led most factory workers to settle in the mandated territories
It drew more people into the cities, especially Sydney and Melbourne
questions.explanation: Protected manufacturing industries, motor vehicle assembly and new consumer goods were concentrated in the capital cities, and suburbs spread as cars and trams allowed. Australia was already one of the most urbanised countries, and this trend continued.

questions.stem: Which policy best shows how governments in the 1920s tried to encourage both manufacturing and rural development?
options: Nationalisation of the banks and a ban on borrowing from overseas
Abolition of the Arbitration Court and a cut to all tariffs on imports
Tariffs for industry alongside loans for irrigation and land settlement
Free trade with Britain and the closure of soldier settlement schemes
questions.explanation: Governments kept high tariffs to protect local manufacturers while borrowing heavily, much of it in London, to fund railways, irrigation and land settlement. This borrowing left Australia exposed when overseas lending stopped in 1929. Bank nationalisation was attempted only in 1947.

questions.stem: Which scientific success of the late 1920s and early 1930s reclaimed large areas of farm land in Queensland and New South Wales?
options: Biological control of prickly pear with the cactoblastis moth
The release of the myxoma virus to control rabbits in 1926
The building of the Snowy Mountains hydro-electric scheme
The introduction of cane toads to control the sugar cane beetles
questions.explanation: The cactoblastis moth, released by the Commonwealth Prickly Pear Board from 1926, destroyed most of the prickly pear that had overrun millions of hectares of Queensland and New South Wales by the early 1930s. Myxomatosis was released in 1950, and cane toads were introduced in 1935 with disastrous results.

questions.stem: At the worst point of the Great Depression in 1932, unemployment among Australian trade union members was about:
options: 60 per cent
30 per cent
10 per cent
5 per cent
questions.explanation: Unemployment among trade unionists peaked at around 30 per cent in 1932, one of the highest rates in the industrial world. Many others were on reduced hours.

questions.stem: During the Depression, unemployed Australians who received government relief, usually food or ration coupons, were said to be:
options: 'on the swag'
'on the susso'
'on the wallaby'
'on the Bradman'
questions.explanation: 'Susso' was short for sustenance, the relief paid in kind or later for relief work. Men who went 'on the wallaby' or carried their swag were travelling in search of work, which is not the same as receiving relief.

questions.stem: Which group was hit especially hard by the Depression because of the collapse in export prices?
options: Car manufacturers, who were banned from selling cars
Wheat and wool farmers, many already in debt
Public servants, whose pay rose during the crisis
Bank shareholders in London, who lost all their savings
questions.explanation: Prices for wheat and wool, Australia's main exports, fell steeply after 1929, leaving many farmers, including soldier settlers, unable to meet debts. Public servants had their pay cut under the Premiers' Plan.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how the Depression affected women in Australia?
options: Women's wages rose above men's because employers preferred to hire female workers
The government paid all married women a weekly allowance from 1930 onwards
Many kept families going on low wages, and women got less relief than men
Women were unaffected because they were barred from paid work throughout the 1930s
questions.explanation: Women's lower pay sometimes kept them in work when men lost jobs, but women received less relief than men, and many struggled to keep households going on very little. No general allowance for married women existed, and women's wages stayed far below men's.

questions.stem: Which Labor prime minister, elected in October 1929, led Australia into the Great Depression?
options: Stanley Bruce
John Curtin
James Scullin
Joseph Lyons
questions.explanation: James Scullin's Labor government took office just before the Wall Street Crash and struggled with a hostile Senate and a conservative Commonwealth Bank board. It split in 1931, and Lyons's United Australia Party won the December 1931 election.

questions.stem: In 1930 Sir Otto Niemeyer of the Bank of England advised Australian governments to:
options: borrow more from London to fund public works
stop paying interest on British loans
print money to pay the unemployed
cut spending and balance their budgets
questions.explanation: Niemeyer argued that Australia had been living beyond its means and must cut spending, wages and borrowing. At a meeting in Melbourne in August 1930, the premiers and the prime minister agreed to balance budgets. Stopping interest payments was Lang's later proposal.

questions.stem: What was the main proposal of the Lang Plan put forward by NSW Premier Jack Lang in 1931?
options: Cut the wages, pensions and spending of all governments by 20 per cent
Hand control of all state finances to the Commonwealth Bank board in Sydney
Raise income taxes sharply to repay all overseas loans within ten years
Stop paying interest to British bondholders until debts were renegotiated
questions.explanation: Lang wanted to suspend interest payments to British bondholders, cut interest on internal debt and expand credit. The 20 per cent cut in government spending was the Premiers' Plan, which Lang rejected and the other governments adopted.

questions.stem: The Premiers' Plan of June 1931 was based on:
options: cuts to government spending, wages and pensions
large public works funded by the issue of new money
the refusal to pay any interest on overseas loans
a new tariff on all British manufactured goods
questions.explanation: Under the Premiers' Plan the Commonwealth and the states agreed to cut government spending by 20 per cent, including wages and pensions, and to reduce interest rates on internal loans and raise taxes. It followed the orthodox deflationary approach of the time.

questions.stem: Why did the NSW Governor, Sir Philip Game, dismiss Premier Jack Lang in May 1932?
options: Lang had lost a vote of no confidence in the NSW Legislative Assembly
Lang had been convicted in court of fraud over the New Guard affair
Lang had announced that New South Wales would secede from the Commonwealth
He judged that Lang had acted illegally over state funds
questions.explanation: Lang defaulted on interest payments, and when the Commonwealth moved to seize state revenue, he instructed public servants not to pay money to it. Game decided Lang was acting illegally and dismissed him on 13 May 1932. Lang's party lost the election that followed.

questions.stem: Joseph Lyons became prime minister in January 1932 after:
options: winning a referendum on the Premiers' Plan held in December 1931
being appointed by the Governor-General after Scullin's dismissal
leaving Labor and leading the new United Australia Party to victory
being chosen by the Labor caucus to replace James Scullin as leader
questions.explanation: Lyons, a Labor minister, left the party over its economic policy and led the new United Australia Party, which won the December 1931 election. Scullin was defeated at the election, not dismissed.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best support the view that political responses to the Depression in Australia were only partly effective?
options: Lang's default on interest payments was supported by the Bank of England in 1931
Recovery began by the mid-1930s, but unemployment stayed high until wartime
The Premiers' Plan was accepted by every government, including Lang's in New South Wales
Unemployment fell to under 2 per cent in 1932 as soon as the Premiers' Plan took effect
questions.explanation: Australia's economy recovered from about 1933, helped by better export prices and a devalued currency, but unemployment remained high through the 1930s and fell sharply only with wartime mobilisation. Lang rejected the Premiers' Plan, and unemployment peaked in 1932.

questions.stem: In 1931 the Commonwealth Arbitration Court cut the basic wage by 10 per cent. Which argument did supporters of this decision make?
options: Lower wages were needed to pay for the new old-age pension scheme
Lower wages would make imports cheaper and reduce the cost of living
Lower costs would help employers keep workers and restore profits
Lower wages would increase spending and so end the Depression quickly
questions.explanation: Supporters, following orthodox economics, believed that reducing labour costs would allow businesses to survive and rehire. Critics, then and since, argued that wage cuts reduced spending and deepened the slump.

questions.stem: The English cricket team's 'Bodyline' tactics in the 1932-33 Ashes series were designed mainly to stop:
options: Don Bradman
Victor Trumper
Bill Woodfull
Richie Benaud
questions.explanation: England captain Douglas Jardine had his fast bowlers, led by Harold Larwood, aim short balls at the batsman's body with a packed leg-side field to curb Bradman's scoring. The tactics caused a diplomatic row and fed Australian nationalism. Woodfull was Australia's captain.

questions.stem: Why did the racehorse Phar Lap become a national hero in the early 1930s?
options: He was the first Australian horse to race in the Olympic Games
He was bred by the Commonwealth government to promote Australian agriculture
He won the Melbourne Cup in every year from 1928 to 1932
His wins, including the 1930 Melbourne Cup, lifted spirits in hard times
questions.explanation: Phar Lap won the 1930 Melbourne Cup and many other races, giving Australians something to celebrate during the Depression. His sudden death in the United States in 1932 caused national grief.

questions.stem: Which event of March 1932 became a symbol of national pride and engineering achievement during the Depression?
options: The opening of the Sydney Harbour Bridge
The opening of Parliament House in Canberra
The completion of the Snowy Mountains Scheme
The opening of the Australian War Memorial
questions.explanation: The Sydney Harbour Bridge opened on 19 March 1932. The ceremony was disrupted when Francis de Groot of the right-wing New Guard cut the ribbon before Premier Lang could. Parliament House in Canberra opened in 1927 and the War Memorial in 1941.

questions.stem: How did the Anzac legend shape Australian identity between the wars?
options: Anzac Day became a holiday in every state, and memorials were built across the nation
Anzac Day was abolished in the 1920s because most returned soldiers rejected it
The legend was confined to Gallipoli veterans and was not part of school teaching
The legend was replaced by a new focus on the Boer War as the nation's founding event
questions.explanation: By 1927 all states observed a public holiday on Anzac Day, and thousands of local memorials were built, along with the Shrine of Remembrance in Melbourne and the Anzac Memorial in Sydney, both opened in 1934. The Australian War Memorial in Canberra opened in 1941.

questions.stem: A historian argues that Australian nationalism in the 1930s was still closely tied to the British Empire. Which evidence best supports this?
options: Australia adopted the Statute of Westminster in 1931 as soon as Britain passed it
The Bodyline row led Australia to cut diplomatic ties with Britain for two years
Australia ended all tariff preferences on British goods after the 1932 Ottawa Conference
Most Australians saw themselves as British, and governments followed Britain abroad
questions.explanation: Many Australians thought of themselves as 'independent Australian Britons', and Lyons's government supported British appeasement. Australia did not adopt the Statute of Westminster until 1942, no ties were cut over Bodyline, and the Ottawa agreements extended imperial preference.

questions.stem: Which development best shows the role of industry in 1930s Australian nationalism?
options: Campaigns urging people to 'buy Australian-made' and the growth of BHP's steelworks
The closure of most factories and a return to rural self-sufficiency in every state
The banning of all foreign films and books by the Lyons government in 1933
The transfer of most manufacturing to Britain under the Ottawa agreements
questions.explanation: Tariffs protected local industry, BHP expanded steel production at Newcastle and took over the Port Kembla works in 1935, and campaigns promoted Australian-made goods as a patriotic choice. Factories did not close en masse, and there was no ban on foreign films.

questions.stem: Which Labor prime minister led Australia from October 1941 through most of the Pacific War?
options: Ben Chifley
John Curtin
Robert Menzies
Arthur Fadden
questions.explanation: John Curtin became prime minister in October 1941 and led the country until his death in July 1945. Menzies and Fadden had led the government before him, and Chifley succeeded him in 1945.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Australian foreign policy in the 1920s and 1930s?
options: It relied on a formal defence treaty with the United States signed in 1922
It aimed to build an alliance with Japan against the Soviet Union in the Pacific
It generally followed Britain and relied on the Singapore naval base for security
It was fully independent and run from Australia's own embassies in every major capital
questions.explanation: Australia relied on imperial defence and the 'Singapore strategy', a promise that the British fleet would come to the Far East in a crisis. It had no legations of its own outside London until 1940 and no treaty with the US before 1951.

questions.stem: In 1938 waterside workers at Port Kembla refused to load pig iron bound for Japan. Why?
options: They objected to the iron being sold below the world price
They wanted all iron exports redirected to Britain instead
They feared it would be used in Japan's war against China
They were demanding higher pay for loading heavy cargo
questions.explanation: The Dalfram dispute was a protest against Japanese aggression in China. Attorney-General Robert Menzies tried to force loading, earning the nickname 'Pig Iron Bob'. The Lyons government still sought to avoid conflict with Japan.

questions.stem: In 1940 the Menzies government opened Australia's first legation in Washington. This showed:
options: Australia's decision to leave the British Commonwealth
a formal military alliance between Australia and the US
the transfer of Australian forces to American command
a growing wish to deal directly with the United States
questions.explanation: Richard Casey became Australia's first minister to the United States in 1940, as Australia began to conduct its own diplomacy. Legations in Tokyo and a high commission in Ottawa followed. A formal alliance came only with ANZUS in 1951.

questions.stem: Curtin wrote in December 1941 that Australia 'looks to America'. Which development of 1942 best shows this new relationship in practice?
options: The signing of the ANZUS Treaty in Washington within weeks of the fall of Singapore
Churchill's decision to send the British fleet to defend Australia from Japanese invasion
MacArthur's appointment as Supreme Commander, South West Pacific Area, based in Australia
Australia's withdrawal from the British Commonwealth and its formal union with the United States
questions.explanation: After the fall of Singapore, MacArthur arrived in Australia in March 1942 and became Supreme Commander of Allied forces in the South West Pacific, with Australian forces under his command. ANZUS was not signed until 1951, and Australia stayed in the Commonwealth.

questions.stem: In 1936 the Lyons government's trade diversion policy damaged relations with the United States because it:
options: banned the export of Australian wool to American mills
refused to repay American loans taken out in the 1920s
ended the landing rights of American airlines in Sydney
restricted American imports to favour British goods
questions.explanation: Trade diversion restricted imports from countries such as the United States and Japan in order to favour British trade. The US responded by blacklisting Australia from its most-favoured-nation treatment, and the dispute dragged on until 1938.

questions.stem: Which statement about Australia's foreign policy under H. V. Evatt in the later 1940s is most accurate?
options: Evatt refused to take part in the San Francisco Conference that founded the United Nations
Evatt promoted the United Nations and was President of its General Assembly in 1948-49
Evatt withdrew Australia from the United Nations because it was dominated by the great powers
Evatt signed a defence treaty with the Netherlands to restore Dutch rule in Indonesia
questions.explanation: As Minister for External Affairs, Evatt was prominent at the San Francisco Conference in 1945, argued for the rights of small and middle powers and served as President of the UN General Assembly in 1948-49. The Chifley government supported Indonesian independence rather than Dutch rule.

questions.stem: Which statement best sums up the change in Australia's foreign policy between 1918 and 1949?
options: From membership of the League towards neutrality in the Second World War
From reliance on Britain to an independent voice and closer ties with the US
From close alliance with the US towards dependence on Britain and the Empire
From isolation from world affairs towards a formal alliance with Japan
questions.explanation: In 1918 Australia followed Britain's lead and relied on imperial defence. The fall of Singapore and the Pacific War made the US Australia's main protector, and by 1949 Australia had its own diplomatic service, an active UN role and was seeking a US alliance, achieved in ANZUS in 1951.
